h: Getting there and exploring the rest of Iona
p: Iona takes a bit of getting to, and that's half its charm. Most visitors head to Oban, take the ferry across to Craignure on Mull, then drive or bus the length of the Ross of Mull to Fionnphort, where the short ferry hops across to Iona. Visitors can't take their cars onto the island, so you'll leave the car at Fionnphort and walk on. Doing it as a day trip from Oban means a long but memorable day, so many people prefer to stay on Mull or Iona itself.

Once you're there, the island is small enough to explore on foot. The ruins of the medieval nunnery sit close to the village, and their quiet gardens are a peaceful spot. Climb Dùn Ì, the island's highest point, for views across to Mull and the scattered islands beyond. On a clear day it's breathtaking.

Iona's beaches are the other big surprise. The north end has white sand and turquoise water that look more Caribbean than Hebridean, while the Bay at the Back of the Ocean on the west coast catches the full sweep of the Atlantic. St Columba's Bay, at the southern tip, is traditionally where the saint landed.

The Iona Community still holds daily worship in the abbey, which adds a living, working feel to an ancient place. In season, boat trips run from Iona and Fionnphort to Staffa, with its famous basalt columns and Fingal's Cave, often with puffins thrown in. Bring a packed lunch, sturdy shoes and a sense of wonder.
